source_refs.note: Topic 23.7.1 (PDF 113); the equations are redrawn. The book numbers the methods i, iii and iv (no ii); the phenyl benzoate example follows the learning outcome.

items: From carboxylic acids and alcohols (Fischer esterification), in acid: CH3CH2COOH + CH3CH2OH <=> CH3CH2COOCH2CH3 + H2O (H+), giving ethyl propanoate. In general RCOOH + HOR' <=> RCOOR' + H2O: the C-OH bond of the acid and the O-H bond of the alcohol break.

From acyl chlorides and alcohols: acyl chlorides react vigorously with alcohols; the reaction goes to completion and does not form an equilibrium mixture: CH3COCl + CH3CH2OH -> CH3COOCH2CH3 + HCl (ethyl ethanoate).
From acyl chlorides and phenol: phenyl esters form when an acyl chloride is warmed with phenol (Chapter 22), e.g. C6H5COCl + C6H5OH -> C6H5COOC6H5 + HCl (phenyl benzoate).

blocks.alt: Top: R-CO-OH + H-O-R' <=> R-CO-O-R' + H2O, with the OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol boxed in orange, and the ethyl propanoate example. Middle: CH3COCl + CH3CH2OH -> CH3COOCH2CH3 + HCl and C6H5COCl + C6H5OH -> C6H5COOC6H5 + HCl, which go to completion. Bottom: hydrolysis of ethyl benzoate and methyl benzoate to benzoic acid and the alcohol.
blocks.caption: Making and hydrolysing esters (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: In esterification the water that forms comes from the OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol. Using an acyl chloride instead of the acid gives a faster, complete reaction because HCl is lost instead of water. Hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification, splitting the ester back into the acid and the alcohol.

blocks.prompt: Why is an acyl chloride often used instead of a carboxylic acid to make an ester?
blocks.explanation: It reacts quickly at room temperature and the reaction goes to completion (HCl escapes), whereas the acid and alcohol give an equilibrium mixture.

items: Acid + alcohol <=> ester + water (H+): C-OH of the acid and O-H of the alcohol break.
Acyl chloride + alcohol or phenol -> ester + HCl, to completion.
